items.passage: Who teaches scales on a bridge in February? Budi did, every Thursday of my fourteenth year, marching me from his flat to the stone span over the canal so that, he said, I could hear the note without a room to flatter it. He stopped me at every sour interval. He would tap the parapet twice, and I would begin again while barges slid underneath and my fingers went white. On the last of those Thursdays he set a coin on the stone and walked off without collecting it. Then he was gone: no letter, no forwarding address, eleven years. When he reappeared one spring, he gave no account of where he had been. I was teaching by then, and on a cold Thursday I had brought my own pupil to the same bridge, telling her that a room would only flatter her. Budi stood a little way off and listened through two scales. He did not tap the parapet once. When we finished, he nodded at my pupil, then at me, and went to buy chestnuts.
items.question: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
options: To recount how a strict teacher shaped the narrator through cold lessons and repeated correction on a bridge
To show how a reunion reveals that the narrator now passes on a method once endured as a student
To describe how a former teacher returns after many years away and offers no account of his absence
To suggest that the narrator's own work as a teacher prompted the former teacher to return after years

items.passage: “Nowhere on this street makes better broth,” I told my sister when she asked why I walked so far for breakfast. For two years I took the same stool at the stall, the one that faced away from the church of my childhood, and Father Bao, who still ate there before morning Mass, took the stool beside the pot. We nodded and did not speak. In March a notice went up on the church gate: he would be sent north after Easter. The following Monday I came twenty minutes earlier than usual. I ordered two bowls, paid for both, and left his with the cook, covered with a saucer to keep the steam in. I did this every morning for three weeks. I did not once go through the gate. On his final morning I turned my stool around, so that it faced the church, and sat there until he came.
items.question: Based on the text, why does the narrator most likely begin arriving early and paying for Bao's bowl?
options: She prefers the stall's broth to the food served elsewhere along the street.
She wants to honor the departing priest in a form that keeps her outside his services.
She has grown used to sharing the stall with the priest during her daily breakfast.
She regrets having stopped attending Mass and hopes to be welcomed back to it.

items.passage: I only need the right angle, Alba told herself each evening as she carried Sunethra's photograph across the road to the soccer field. The picture was older than either of their houses: a dirt pitch, a crooked goal, a thin boy in the goalmouth whom Sunethra had once identified, through the wall they shared, as her husband. Alba would hold the print at arm's length and step left or right until the goalposts lined up. On the second evening she found the spot and marked the near post with a stub of chalk. She came back the next evening anyway, and the nine after that, always just as the streetlights flickered on, the minute Sunethra's bus let out at the corner. Boys shouted for the ball around her. On the twelfth evening Sunethra stopped at the fence with her shopping. Alba did not cross to her. She stood by the chalk mark and held the photograph up, angled toward the road.
items.question: Based on the text, why does Alba most likely keep returning to the field after the second evening?
options: She wants to find the exact place on the field where the photograph was taken.
She has come to enjoy spending evenings on the field among the boys playing there.
She hopes to give her neighbor an occasion to view the pictured place alongside her.
She feels guilty about keeping the photograph and wants to return it without speaking.

items.passage: Years later, the binder on Peitavas Street still remembered the gardener who came in with a ledger wrapped in sacking. Stanislav had kept that book for the old owner of the house on the hill for thirty-one seasons, writing each planting in a narrow hand and heading every page with the owner's initials, as he had been taught. The spine is splitting, he told the binder; it will not last another winter. That was true. He had carried it in the week after the new owner, Marta, signed for the house, and not before, though the spine had been splitting for years. He asked that the old pages be resewn exactly as they were. Then he asked for forty blank leaves to be added behind them. When the book was ready, he did not take it to his shed. He walked it up the hill, set it on Marta's kitchen table, and laid his pencil across the first empty page.
items.question: Based on the text, why does Stanislav most likely have the ledger rebound when he does?
options: He worries that the ledger's damaged spine will not survive the coming winter.
He wishes to preserve the record of seasons he kept for the house's former owner.
He fears that the new owner will dismiss him unless he can prove his long service.
He intends to hand the new owner a way to continue the record kept before her.

items.passage: Once the service ended, Nalani and I walked to our grandfather's radio shop because neither of us had a key to anywhere else. Same bell over the door. Same smell of solder and dust. Same calendar, stopped at a March four years gone. Nalani tested the counter with one finger and reported that it was sticky, which it had always been. I reported that the clock was slow, which it had also always been. We took turns naming things. At the back bench sat a transistor set with its case open, a tag in his handwriting tied to the dial: Koa, Tuesday. I did not read the rest of the tag. Nalani found the soldering iron and plugged it in from habit, then stood holding it while it warmed. After a while she reached over, unplugged it, and coiled the cord around her hand three times before setting it in its tray.
items.question: Which choice best describes the overall tone of the text?

items.passage: “Take the clock, and I shall have the chairs,” Kwesi said, as though we were dealing cards. We had taken two cells in the monastery guesthouse above Taipei to settle our mother's house on paper, the brothers having lent us their long table and a pot of tea that never seemed to cool. Kwesi kept the list. I kept the pen. Rugs, mine; lamps, his; the copper kettle, to be sold. We went down the page at a good pace, and the bell for vespers rang twice before we reached the last line, which read only: erhu, to Meilin. I had never played it. Kwesi had played it every evening of our childhood, standing at the window while I did my sums. He passed me the list without remark. That night I carried the instrument along the cloister and set it, bow and all, outside his door.

items.passage: Three rules governed the reading room on the second floor: no food, no phones, no voices above a whisper. Jonas kept all three, and when he needed Yusuf's attention he touched the edge of the table and murmured Ustaz, as he had since their first rehearsal eight years before, though Yusuf was barely older. They came most afternoons to copy out parts, the oud case propped between their chairs. That Thursday an envelope slid from the case's lid pocket: a festival in Lyon, addressed to Yusuf alone, offering a solo evening and a fee for one. Jonas read it, folded it along its creases, and returned it to the pocket. He said nothing. At four, the hour they usually packed up together, he copied out his own part of their new piece twice, left one copy on Yusuf's side of the table with the tempo markings filled in, and walked down the stairs ahead of him.

Jonas is a partner prepared to absorb a loss so that Yusuf can advance.

items.passage: A wall telephone hung beside the blackboard in Room 4, beige and seldom used. On her first morning Mira wrote her name on the board, and Hassan, from the back row, copied it into his notebook as Frau Lehrerin and did not look up again. He answered when called on. He called her Frau Lehrerin when he answered. In the second week a form from the immigration office lay on her desk; in the box marked contact number, the school's extension had been written in her handwriting. After that, Mira took her lunch at the desk instead of in the staff room. On Friday she missed the faculty meeting and received a note about it from the director, which she folded into her grammar book. When the telephone finally rang at ten past four, she lifted the receiver, listened, and held it out across the empty front row toward Hassan without saying a word.

items.passage: Saturdays belong to the market. Renata pushes the wheelchair between the stalls, and her mother, who has called her señora since the wedding, points with her cane at what she will not eat. Not the yuca; it is for other people's kitchens. Not the black beans; her own mother made lentils. Renata pays for both anyway and hangs the bags on the chair's handles. At home there is one table and two ways of setting it, and on alternate Sundays the lentils win. This week the coin purse her mother keeps inside her sleeve is lighter by the price of a pound of beans, and the bag Renata finds on the counter, knotted the old way, was not bought by Renata. Her mother says nothing about it. At dinner she lays the lentil spoon in the drawer and sets the ladle beside Renata's pot, handle turned toward her own plate.

options: The mother is a parent who keeps a formal distance from her married daughter.
The mother is a parent who quietly yields her own custom to make room for Renata's.

items.passage: Cloth tape, yellowed and marked in both inches and Chinese cun, hung around my mother's neck from the week we rented the farmhouse west of Shanghai. Yuying measured everything herself: the parlor, the courtyard, the width of the door through which my bridal chair would have to pass. When I offered to hold the other end, she pinned it under her shoe instead. We expected the groom's aunt to arrive with opinions, and in the second week she did, stepping down from a cart with lists of her own. That afternoon in the courtyard my mother unwound the tape and, without a word, held out the brass end to her. The two of them walked the length of the wall together, calling numbers to each other. On the morning the aunt left, my mother wound the tape into a tight coil, tied it with red thread, and set it in the older woman's hand.
items.question: In the text, the tape measure most likely represents
options: the careful planning needed to fit a wedding into a small rented house.
the mother's wish to keep each decision about the wedding in her own hands.
the mother's control of the wedding, which she comes to place in another's keeping.
the tension between two older women that is mended as the wedding nears.

items.passage: Diesel and wet wool, and under them the faint smell of tea from Kenji's flask: the last bus out of Asahikawa always smelled the same in January. Hana boarded two stops after him, as she had every night that week, carrying the same wrapped cup. She had bought it at his shop in the autumn. There was a hairline crack along its rim, she said, and she wished to exchange it. He said there was no crack. She said there had been one since the day she bought it. Neither mentioned the shop's other business, the debt her brother had left on Kenji's books the year before. On the fourth night, near Biei, Kenji took the cup from her, unwrapped it, and tipped it under the dim ceiling bulb until the line showed. He did not hand it back. ### lit40-hard-02-041 — skill central_ideas_details · 유형 main_idea_or_purpose
[지문]
Who teaches scales on a bridge in February? Budi did, every Thursday of my fourteenth year, marching me from his flat to the stone span over the canal so that, he said, I could hear the note without a room to flatter it. He stopped me at every sour interval. He would tap the parapet twice, and I would begin again while barges slid underneath and my fingers went white. On the last of those Thursdays he set a coin on the stone and walked off without collecting it. Then he was gone: no letter, no forwarding address, eleven years. When he reappeared one spring, he gave no account of where he had been. I was teaching by then, and on a cold Thursday I had brought my own pupil to the same bridge, telling her that a room would only flatter her. Budi stood a little way off and listened through two scales. He did not tap the parapet once. When we finished, he nodded at my pupil, then at me, and went to buy chestnuts.

[질문] Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
A) To recount how a strict teacher shaped the narrator through cold lessons and repeated correction on a bridge
B) To show how a reunion reveals that the narrator now passes on a method once endured as a student
C) To describe how a former teacher returns after many years away and offers no account of his absence
D) To suggest that the narrator's own work as a teacher prompted the former teacher to return after years

[표시된 정답] B
[해설]
지문 앞부분은 Budi가 다리 위에서 엄격하게 레슨하던 기억(사건 1)이고, 뒷부분은 몇 년 뒤 화자가 자기 학생을 같은 다리로 데려와 같은 말을 하는 장면을 Budi가 지켜보는 재회(사건 2)다. 두 사건을 겹쳐 읽으면 화자가 학생 시절 견뎠던 방식을 이제 스스로 물려주고 있다는 관계가 드러나므로 B가 정답이다. A는 사건 1만, C는 사건 2만 요약한 부분 요지다. D는 두 사건을 연결하지만 화자의 교직이 Budi의 귀환을 불러왔다는 인과는 지문에 근거가 없다.

[질문] As used in the text, the phrase “a column of figures written on river ice” most nearly suggests
A) a tally of debts between them that will not settle into a final sum.
B) a coldness between them that has grown out of the harsh winters they shared.
C) an account between them so fragile that a single word might break it apart.

[표시된 정답] A
[해설]
비유 앞에서 두 사람은 서로를 위해 각각 발가락과 손을 잃는 불균등한 희생을 치렀고, Farhad는 손가락으로 셈을 하다가 합계에 이를 때마다 처음부터 다시 센다. 강 얼음 위의 숫자 열은 이처럼 확정된 합계로 굳지 않고 계속 흔들리는 빚의 셈을 뜻하므로 A가 정답이다. 비유 뒤에 Shirin이 다친 발의 끈을 필요 이상으로 조이는 동작도 셈이 끝나지 않았음을 암시한다. B는 차가움, C는 깨지기 쉬움이라는 다른 속성만 골랐고, D는 문자 그대로의 기록으로 읽었다.
